clue.text: Congestion in throat after large measure of vodka, say?

blocks.note: a whole bottle is a large measure of a spirit such as vodka; 'say' flags the example
the neck holds the throat; to neck a drink is also to swallow it

explanation.surface: A drinker gulps a big slug of vodka and feels a blockage in the throat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places the throat word behind the vodka measure, and a bottle's narrow neck is itself the picture of congestion.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottleneck is a narrow point where traffic or flow piles up, which is exactly congestion.

clue.text: Academic award alongside personal project

blocks.note: Bachelor of Arts, a university degree
by means beside or alongside, as in 'sit by me'

explanation.surface: A student's degree is earned alongside some pet project of their own.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a scheme 'my baby' is an idiom for a pet project one cherishes and is responsible for.

clue.text: Saw, for example, cash being lifted

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting the word lets it read from the bottom upwards, so it runs backwards

blocks.note: loot is slang for money or cash

explanation.surface: Something such as a saw, perhaps, while some money is being stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' reads like the past tense of see; here it is the cutting implement, given as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is one example of a hand implement used for work, so it is a member of that category.

clue.text: Efficient – as a political rescue package?

blocks.note: first meaning: designed to cut down effort and work
second, punning meaning: rescuing Labour, the British political party

explanation.walkthrough: Labour is one of Britain's two main political parties, so a package that bails it out is one 'saving Labour'; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Labour-saving devices reduce the human work needed for a task, so they make it efficient.

clue.text: Aristocrats gathered up by damsel, bonded

indicators.note: the letters are collected from inside the run of words that follows, spanning two of them
in a down entry, going up means reading the collected letters from bottom to top, so backwards

blocks.note: the tail of damsel joined to the start of bonded

explanation.surface: Noblemen are rounded up and tied together by a young lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobles are people of high hereditary rank, the same class as aristocrats.

clue.text: Note theatre-goers originally in stitches

indicators.note: originally points to the very start, so only the opening letter of the phrase is kept
one piece is placed inside the other, sitting within its letters

blocks.note: the first letter of theatre-goers
crochet is needlework made of looped stitches

explanation.surface: Theatre audiences are reduced to helpless laughter by some written remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in stitches' suggests laughter, but stitches is the needlework word that wraps the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A crotchet is a musical note worth one beat, called a quarter note in American usage.

clue.text: On holiday, a king of Mercia

blocks.note: someone off work is on holiday
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch of old Mercia is away on his holidays.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Offa ruled the Anglo-Saxon realm of Mercia in the eighth century and built the dyke named after him.

clue.text: Entertainment centre just reduced to tiny pieces

blocks.note: just and fair both mean impartial
ground, as coffee is, means crushed into small particles

explanation.surface: A leisure complex is simply smashed to bits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just' looks like an adverb meaning 'simply', but it is the adjective meaning impartial.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground is the site of rides and stalls, a place built for amusement and fun.

clue.text: Changes man set about to conceal repair

indicators.note: about suggests turning things around, so the letters are rearranged
the rearranged letters hide another word inside them

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to mend is to repair

explanation.surface: A man sets out to cover up a repair job, perhaps botched.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged six letters split after their first letter to take in the repair word.
explanation.definitionFit: Amendments are alterations made to a text or law, so they are changes.

clue.text: Possible description of commentary – in boxing?

definitions.text: Possible description of commentary – in boxing?

blocks.note: surface reading: a running commentary that reports every detail as it happens
setter's reading: in a boxing match the commentator literally describes each punch thrown in turn

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means a detailed, step-by-step account; the boxing hint makes it literal, with each punch a 'blow'.
explanation.definitionFit: A blow-by-blow account narrates events in full sequence, which suits a detailed commentary.

clue.text: Fee payable for misdemeanour, OK

blocks.note: first meaning: a monetary penalty for a minor offence
second meaning: all right, acceptable

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase about a charge being acceptable; the comma splits two unrelated meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for a monetary penalty and an adjective meaning satisfactory or alright.

clue.text: Party issue shut up writer

blocks.note: a ball is a formal dance party
a point at issue is a matter under discussion
to pen an animal is to shut it up in an enclosure

explanation.surface: A political party's policy matter silences an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writer' looks like a person, but it is the implement used for writing.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballpoint pen is a common writing implement, so it is a writer in the sense of a thing that writes.

clue.text: Very quick, huge car sped round corner, finally

indicators.note: sending the letters round suggests whirling them about into a new order
finally means only the closing letter of the word before it is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged
the last letter of corner

explanation.surface: A big car tears round a bend at the end of a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'huge' tempts as SUPER, but every word from huge to sped goes into the mix, plus the final letter of corner.
explanation.definitionFit: Supercharged means boosted with extra power or energy, so moving or performing very fast.

clue.text: Worker bound to produce gymnastic feat

blocks.note: a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand
to bound is to leap or spring

explanation.surface: An employee is obliged to put on an athletic display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound' reads as 'obliged', but it is the verb for a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: A handspring is a gymnastic move where the body flips over onto the hands and back to the feet.

clue.text: Thoroughly deserved we understood, first in literature bagged

indicators.note: first in points to the opening letter of the next word only
something bagged has been put inside a holder, so one letter sits within the others

blocks.note: taken as written
learned, as a past tense, means grasped or understood
the first letter of literature

explanation.surface: A literary prize was truly merited, as we realised once it was won.
explanation.walkthrough: The single letter is tucked in between the two words just after WE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something well-earned has been fully merited by effort, so it is thoroughly deserved.

clue.text: Hostile, a part of poem?

blocks.note: taken as written
a verse is a stanza, one section of a poem

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a stretch of a poem is unfriendly.
explanation.definitionFit: To be averse to something is to oppose or dislike it, so one is hostile towards it.

clue.text: Congratulations certainly not rare!

blocks.note: first meaning: an exclamation of praise
second meaning: of steak, cooked right through, the opposite of rare

explanation.walkthrough: 'rare' reads as 'uncommon', so the praise sounds frequent; it is the steak sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a cry of praise for an achievement and the term for meat cooked thoroughly.

clue.text: Feed in item of fruit for primate

indicators.note: one word is placed within the other, inside its letters

blocks.note: to feed is to eat
a single grape is one item of fruit

explanation.surface: Instructions to put a piece of fruit in front of a monkey at feeding time.
explanation.walkthrough: The eating word splits the fruit after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Great apes, such as gorillas and chimpanzees, are a family of large primates.

clue.text: Shipment remarkably found next to shop

blocks.note: a deli, short for delicatessen, is a food shop
remarkably and very both mean to a high degree

explanation.surface: A consignment turns up, surprisingly, beside a store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'next to' places the degree word after the shop word.
explanation.definitionFit: A delivery is a consignment of goods brought to someone, which is a shipment.

clue.text: Small flier then, or cuckoo

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters before it are jumbled out of their sense

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Pick a little bird, then, or else a cuckoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuckoo' sits beside 'flier' as if it were another bird; it means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A hornet is a large wasp, a flying insect that is small compared with a bird or plane.

clue.text: Aboard ship, want casual attire

indicators.note: being aboard means sitting inside a vessel, so one word goes within another

blocks.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
to want is to lack

explanation.surface: On a ship, someone wants to dress down.
explanation.definitionFit: Slacks are loose everyday trousers, a kind of informal clothing.

clue.text: A breeze travelling behind flier, did you say?

indicators.note: asking what was said points to how a word sounds rather than how it is written
behind sends the travelling word to stand after the flier word, so it comes second

blocks.note: a plane is an aircraft, a flier
sailing means travelling by water

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a breeze is travelling behind an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breeze' suggests wind for sailing, but it means something easy; 'behind' puts the travel word after the flier.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain sailing is an idiom for something easy and trouble-free, as is a breeze.

clue.text: Follow story that's read out

indicators.note: reading something out loud means only the sound of the word counts

blocks.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: Keep up with a narrative that is being recited.
explanation.definitionFit: To tail someone is to follow them closely, usually covertly, as a detective does.

clue.text: Shame it is entertained by outsiders in party

indicators.note: a guest who is entertained is taken in, so one piece is held inside another
outsiders means the letters on the outside edges, the first and last

blocks.note: the first and last letters of party
taken as written

explanation.surface: It's a disgrace that a gatecrasher was entertained at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Shame here is the regret of 'what a shame', not disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: 'What a shame' and 'what a pity' are interchangeable, both expressing regret.

clue.text: Some sensational island off Scotland

indicators.note: some means just a portion, so the letters come from inside a word

blocks.note: letters seven to ten of sensational

explanation.surface: An amazing island lies off the Scottish coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a small island in the Inner Hebrides, off Scotland's west coast, famous for its abbey.

clue.text: Ancient caskets in wreckage of a cargo ship

indicators.note: wreckage is something broken up, so the letters that follow are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Old coffins are found among the remains of a sunken freighter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarcophagi, plural of sarcophagus, are stone coffins used in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome.

clue.text: Initials of Giotto on drawings seen in gallery

definitions.note: singular in the clue, but the answer is the plural-form name for that one gallery

indicators.note: initials are opening letters, so only the first letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of Giotto
the first letter of on
the first letter of drawings
the first letter of seen

explanation.surface: Giotto's monogram is spotted on sketches displayed in an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gallery' suggests an art gallery for Giotto's sketches; in British theatres the gods are the highest, cheapest gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: The gods is the informal name for the uppermost balcony of seats in a theatre.

clue.text: Only pearls flawed, as far as one is concerned

definitions.text: as far as one is concerned

indicators.note: flawed means imperfect or damaged, so the letters are put into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A jeweller's opinion: only these pearls have defects.
explanation.definitionFit: Personally signals one's own view, meaning speaking for oneself or in one's own opinion.
